fn.p: The underlying conflict mechanisms between commercial efficacies and systemic risks across these dimensions are further elaborated in the main text.

sec.p: During service delivery, a goal divergence persists between algorithmic operational logic and human-centric emotional demands. By batch-generating standardized text and multimodal content, algorithmic agents effectively minimize corporate content production costs and tourists’ information retrieval time (Bilgihan et al., 2024). However, when technological intervention extends into service touchpoints requiring high empathy—such as customer complaint resolution or personalized care—algorithmic models lacking embodied experience struggle to offer authentic emotional feedback (Yaşar and Yayla, 2025). Once service recipients detect the computational essence driving this emotional feedback, the pre-existing foundation of trust faces deconstruction, eliciting the phenomenon of algorithm aversion (Tan et al., 2025). This mechanism indicates that a technological logic singularly pursuing operational efficiency dilutes the service attributes emphasizing authentic interpersonal connections within the tourism industry when handling high-involvement emotional labor (Xu et al., 2026). Failure to meticulously delineate the boundaries of responsibility between AI and human employees in emotional transmission exposes enterprises to the risks of service homogenization and brand equity erosion (Zhao et al., 2024).

The coexistence of efficacy and risk translates into ambivalent and vacillating user attitudes toward technology acceptance. To secure highly precise, customized itinerary recommendations, tourists must input sensitive information—including budgets and personal preferences—into the algorithmic system (Domínguez and Rodríguez, 2025). Confronting opaque black-box algorithms, privacy and security anxieties amplify tourists’ threat perceptions, driving them to adopt defensive behaviors while extracting informational convenience (Yhee et al., 2025; Fakfare et al., 2025b) While the highly anthropomorphic interaction styles of algorithmic agents foster preliminary parasocial interactions, the blurred boundaries between their instrumental and social attributes heighten the instability of user psychological expectations (Chen et al., 2025). As tourists repeatedly weigh efficiency gains against privacy anxieties, and emotional expectations against authenticity deprivation, their adoption behavior toward generative systems manifests a high degree of situational dependency (Volchek and Ivanov, 2024; Xiao et al., 2026). This ambivalent acceptance behavior clarifies why GenAI achieves widespread adoption in pre-trip information searches yet frequently encounters resistance during deep emotional interactions and final decision-making phases (Água et al., 2025).

sec.title: Theoretical implications
sec.p: The review carries four theoretical implications. First, it shows that the theories currently invoked in GenAI research are complementary mechanisms of one socio-technical system rather than competing lenses: TAM and UTAUT operate at the utility layer, Conservation of Resources and Technology Threat Avoidance theories at the appraisal layer, and Parasocial Interaction, Expectancy Violation, and embodied-cognition perspectives at the emotional layer of service encounters. Second, the evidence specifies the boundary conditions under which efficiency gains turn into risks: task involvement, emotional intensity, disclosure, digital literacy, and organizational support determine which mechanisms dominate. Third, the authenticity conflict extends authenticity theorizing to algorithmic service contexts, suggesting that interactional authenticity—rather than objective authenticity—is the dimension most exposed to machine intervention. Fourth, the ambivalent acceptance pattern documented across studies calibrates technology acceptance models for generative systems: adoption and aversion are not opposite poles of one continuum but situational responses that can coexist within the same user.

sec.title: Practical managerial implications: constructing a responsible human-in-the-loop framework
sec.p: Intelligent transformation reconstructs the service delivery logic of the tourism industry. To navigate the conflict between efficiency expansion and emotional deprivation, tourism enterprises should implement a tiered human-in-the-loop framework in which the degree of automation varies with the stakes of the decision. Routine information retrieval, standardized inquiries, and draft content generation can be automated, with human verification applied to the output; decisions that affect service recovery, personalized care, pricing, or legal exposure require explicit human approval before execution; and escalation is mandatory whenever the system encounters emotional distress, complaints involving liability, or requests outside its trained domain. The framework should also specify authority and accountability: frontline employees hold the authority to reject an AI output, managers hold escalation authority, and the organization—not the algorithm—carries responsibility for errors, so that authority and liability are aligned rather than left ambiguous.

Human involvement is not by itself a guarantee of quality. Employees may accept AI recommendations automatically, lack the expertise to detect errors, or become dependent on generated outputs. The framework therefore embeds supporting safeguards: audit procedures that log AI decisions and human overrides, privacy controls that enforce data minimization and purpose limitation, correction mechanisms that route detected errors back into prompt and workflow redesign, employee training on the system’s failure modes, and continuous monitoring of accuracy, fairness, and escalation rates. The resulting allocation is summarized in Table 6. On the consumer side, managers should clearly label algorithmically generated content on interactive interfaces and grant users actual control over the scope of data access (Yhee et al., 2025; Fakfare et al., 2025b). Disclosure policies, however, are double-edged: labeling may improve transparency while simultaneously increasing algorithm aversion, because disclosed AI authorship lowers perceived authenticity and, in some studies, reduces persuasion (Tan et al., 2025; Carvalho et al., 2025). Disclosure should therefore be combined with demonstrated human oversight rather than treated as a standalone remedy.

sec.title: Reflexive critique of methodological limitations and future exploratory directions
sec.p: The existing literature relies heavily on cross-sectional questionnaires and static technology acceptance models, remaining disproportionately concentrated in pre-trip, online settings. To address these gaps, we propose five research priorities, each outlining a specific inquiry, theoretical lens, and methodological approach:

list-item.p: Disclosure and Trust Mechanisms: Under what conditions does disclosing AI authorship strengthen rather than weaken consumer trust? Grounded in expectancy violation theory and algorithm aversion research, future scenario-based and field experiments should manipulate the timing, framing, and source of disclosure. This individual-level focus within marketing and service recovery contexts will help identify the boundary conditions of transparency, reconciling the contradictory findings documented in Table 5.

AI-Generated Service Recovery: How does service failure severity alter consumer reactions to AI-generated recovery messages? By integrating justice theory with expectancy violation theory, experimental designs crossing failure severity with message authorship can clarify when human-led recovery remains indispensable and when AI drafts suffice.

Spatial Redistribution of Tourism Demand: Does GenAI steer tourists toward lesser-known destinations or reinforce popularity bias? Utilizing platform-level recommendation logs and quasi-experimental designs, researchers can test whether interface interventions mitigate the concentration effects (Section 5.1), thereby linking algorithmic design directly to destination-level outcomes.

Employee Expertise and Cognitive Dependence: How does repeated GenAI use affect employees’ expertise, decision quality, and cognitive dependence over time? Drawing on conservation of resources theory and skill-based views of work, longitudinal field studies in hotel and travel agency settings are needed to trace the long-term accumulation of benefits and the potential erosion of organizational capabilities.

Equity and Societal Consequences: The current corpus is notably thin regarding cultural differences, language inequalities, digital literacy, and regulatory environments, and silent on long-term socio-environmental impacts. Future efforts should employ comparative cross-cultural studies, small-firm case studies, and life-cycle assessments of AI infrastructure to connect this review’s framework with broader social sustainability agendas.

sec.p: Methodologically, future research should move beyond pre-trip digital interfaces: on-trip studies that pair conversational agents with IoT sensors or embodied systems remain scarce (40 publications), and field experiments with behavioral and physiological measures would test whether self-reported scales diverge from actual adoption behavior. Combined with the cross-database tracking strategy recommended in the limitations, these designs would test and extend the socio-technical framework developed in this review.

sec.title: Limitations of the study
sec.p: This systematic literature review entails limitations. First, although the search covered the Web of Science Core Collection and Scopus, relevant work in specialized information systems and computer science outlets, conference repositories, and preprint servers may have been missed, and backward and forward citation searching was not performed. Second, the search strings consisted of English terms, and the retrieved records were predominantly in English (1,492 of 1,500 Web of Science records), so findings may not capture patterns reported in other languages or local journals. Third, the static cutoff of September 9, 2026 means that the most recent developments fall outside the sample. Fourth, although a design-sensitive quality appraisal weighted the interpretation of the evidence, 54 publications (11.7%) were appraised as methodologically weak, and some thematic conclusions rest on comparatively small evidence bases (e.g., 73 publications for the organizational theme). Subsequent systematic reviews should combine multilingual search strategies across multiple databases with dynamic tracking mechanisms and backward citation searching to continuously refine and expand the framework established in this review.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: This review synthesized 461 publications on generative artificial intelligence in tourism and hospitality, published between 2021 and September 2026 and identified through the Web of Science Core Collection and Scopus. Its primary contribution is an efficacy-risk hedging framework: application-level benefits on the demand and supply sides, systemic ethical risks, and the authenticity conflict are integrated within one socio-technical account, with each thematic claim anchored in article-level evidence counts and a design-sensitive quality appraisal.

Three principal findings follow. First, GenAI’s value creation is concentrated in information-intensive tasks—information search and itinerary generation, marketing content, and back-office functions—documented by 265 and 229 publications on the demand and supply sides, respectively. Second, these gains are systematically accompanied by risks: hallucination and popularity bias, privacy trade-offs, and practitioner deskilling appear as consistent rather than isolated findings across 112, 83, and 73 publications. Third, in emotionally charged service encounters, machine-generated empathy frequently elicits expectancy violations and algorithm aversion (201 publications), so that the authenticity conflict—rather than efficiency—sets the boundary of GenAI’s value in hospitality. The tiered human-in-the-loop model translates these findings into governance practice.
